sb_prompt: DISCUSS WITH THE OTHER CALLER WHETHER THERE IS SOMETHING SERIOUSLY WRONG WITH OUR PUBLIC SCHOOL SYSTEMS TODAYY
turns: Oh, hi! Yeah, actually, that is exactly why I called. It feels like our public schools are just falling apart these days. My kids are supposed to be getting a solid education, but honestly, they come home barely knowing anything. It's not even about money or resources necessarily, it's just that the expectations seem so low compared to how hard my parents had to work in their day. Like, do you ever feel like the teachers are just letting them get away with not doing the work?

That is a tough spot to be in, honestly. I get what you're saying about the comparison with your parents' day, but I think it might be unfair to just blame the teachers. From what I've seen at my son's school, it's often more about the kids themselves today. They seem way more distracted by their phones than anything else, and honestly, a lot of them just don't seem to care about the work anymore. It's less that the teachers are letting them get away with it and more that the students are actively resisting any real effort to engage, which makes it incredibly hard for the teachers to push them.

Oh, I totally get where you're coming from with the phones being a huge distraction, honestly. My own daughter literally just put her head down at the desk the other day because she was on her iPad instead of writing, and the teacher just sighed and moved on without saying anything. It really does feel like everyone just gave up on actually stopping it. But I'm kind of curious, though, do you think the teachers are just too scared to actually discipline them? Because it feels like if anyone did try to make them do the work, the parents would get mad or complain, so the teachers end up just letting it slide to keep the peace. It's frustrating because I remember when I was in high school, we didn't have cell phones at all, and everyone had to actually pay attention just to pass.

That is a really fair point about the fear factor, and honestly, that dynamic between parents and administration probably plays a bigger role in the "giving up" attitude than the kids themselves. I haven't seen a teacher get in trouble for enforcing a phone ban yet, but I do wonder if the issue is more about what the schools are prioritizing now rather than just discipline. Do you think the curriculum itself has gotten watered down to a point where kids just aren't challenged enough to care, or is it mostly that they're just looking for a way out of the grind? I feel like my parents' generation was taught to work hard because there wasn't really a choice, whereas today, if you don't want to do the work, there are literally too many distractions to make you do it.

That is such a good point about the curriculum being watered down, honestly, because I think you're totally right that if the work isn't challenging enough, why would anyone bother trying? It feels like schools are just checking boxes to keep everyone happy instead of actually pushing kids to learn hard things. My daughter came home last week saying her history class was just watching videos on the computer with no notes to take, and I was so confused because my dad had to memorize all those dates just to pass a test. It seems like nobody is holding anyone accountable anymore, whether it's the teachers, the parents, or the kids themselves. Do you think it's possible that the whole system just lost its way, or is it just that society has gotten too soft on everyone?

That is a really valid observation about the whole system potentially losing its way, and I actually think you hit the nail on the head when you mentioned society getting too soft; I feel like we've collectively decided that "being happy" is more important than "being prepared." But I'm also worried that by watering down the curriculum to avoid conflict, we aren't just making kids comfortable, we're actually robbing them of the critical thinking skills they need to survive in the real world. My own parents always forced us to sit through the boring parts of the textbook, and while it was tedious, that's where the real learning happened. Do you think the solution is for schools to start enforcing stricter standards again, even if it means some parents complain, or do you feel like the digital generation just operates on a completely different set of rules that we can't really adapt to?

Yeah, I think you hit the nail on the head about the "being happy" thing because honestly, it does feel like schools are more focused on making sure nobody gets mad than on actually teaching kids how to think for themselves. But I'm not sure I think the digital generation operates on a completely different set of rules that we can't adapt to; I think it's more that they just haven't learned how to sit still or focus long enough to get through the boring parts yet, even if they have the potential to learn it if we push them hard enough. It's scary because my own dad used to say that the only way to survive is to be able to figure things out yourself without needing a video tutorial, and if we let them off the hook now, how are they supposed to handle a job or a crisis later? Do you think there's any way to bring back that old-school pressure without just becoming a tyrant, or do you think we've already lost that window of opportunity forever?

Yeah, I hear you on the "old-school pressure" thing, and honestly, I'm terrified that we might have missed that window forever too. It feels like we're at this tipping point where if we try to force that rigid structure back in, we might just alienate the kids entirely and make the school climate so toxic that it becomes a war zone in every classroom. But I do think there's a middle ground somewhere, right? Maybe it's not about going back to 1990s punishment, but about finding ways to teach them the discipline to actually engage with the digital tools they love instead of letting the tools control them. Like, instead of banning the phones, what if we trained them to use that focus and that instant access to research for actual deep-dive projects rather than just endless scrolling? Do you think we could pivot to that kind of "high-tech discipline" approach, or do you feel like the damage is already done and they've completely lost the ability to do anything other than consume content?

I think you might be onto something with that "high-tech discipline" idea, honestly, because part of me wants to believe that if we just showed them how to use those phones for real learning, they'd actually start caring about it. But I'm kind of stuck on whether it's too late to teach them how to focus long enough to start with a deep-dive project when they're used to getting everything in a ten-second video. It feels like if we try to pivot that way, we'd have to retrain every teacher and maybe even rewrite some curricula, which sounds like a massive headache for a mom who just wants her kid to actually learn something today. Do you really think schools have the resources or the time to do that kind of thing right now, or do you think by the time we figure it out, the kids will just have already graduated and we'll be stuck with a generation that can't read a textbook without checking their phone first?

I get that retraining every teacher sounds like a nightmare right now, and honestly, that's probably why we haven't tried it yet—it's just too much work for the system. But I'm not sure we have to wait until they graduate to start shifting things; some of the smaller progressive schools I know are already piloting these tech-integrated projects where the phones are mandatory tools, not distractions, and the engagement levels are actually higher than the traditional lecture rooms. So maybe it's not that the damage is done, but that the old models are just broken and we need to build a new engine before we can drive anywhere. Do you think there are any specific examples of schools doing this successfully that you've seen, or do you feel like the idea just sounds too idealistic for the current budget constraints?

Oh wow, that is actually super interesting that you're seeing schools where they make the phones mandatory tools; honestly, that sounds like a huge relief because the only "success stories" I've heard about usually involve huge budget cuts or private donations, so it really does feel like too much for a regular district to just pull off right now. I guess I have been assuming that if the students were given the tools to actually research and write instead of just scrolling TikTok, the teachers would have to spend hours every day supervising them and managing their behavior, which is something most of them don't have time for since they're already drowning in paperwork and testing requirements. Do you think those pilots you mentioned are actually proving that the kids can stick with a long-term project, or are they still just letting them watch short clips but calling it "research"?

That is a really fair concern about the teachers drowning in paperwork, and honestly, if those pilots are just repackaging short clips as "research," then we're just sticking to the old broken model. But from what I've seen in those specific projects, it's not about cutting corners; it's actually the opposite—they're forcing the students to do the heavy lifting because the digital tools require them to cite sources, debate in real-time, and actually synthesize information rather than just passively watching. The engagement is higher precisely because the barrier to entry is active participation, not just clicking a button. I think the key is that the teachers in those successful pilots have actually had to take some of the administrative burden off to make room for this kind of project-based work, which is exactly the change the system needs to happen. It feels like a risky pivot, but maybe that's the only way we stop the "check the box" mentality you mentioned earlier and actually get kids to read a textbook without reaching for their phone first.

That actually makes a lot of sense, because if they really had to force them to do the heavy lifting and cite sources instead of just clicking, maybe the teachers wouldn't have to do so much of the boring prep work themselves. I guess I just feel like we're in a weird spot where if we try to make them work harder like that, the parents are going to freak out because their kids aren't getting an easy A anymore. It's just a scary thought that we might have to fight the whole system to get them to actually read a whole chapter without their thumbs always on the screen. Do you think it's worth starting that fight in your area, or do you think it's just not going to happen where I live?

Honestly, I don't think it's worth starting a fight where I live because the political climate here is just too risk-averse; if I tried to push for that kind of accountability, I probably wouldn't get more than a few nods from the board members before they'd revert back to the status quo to keep the parents happy. It feels like we're stuck in this cycle where the only thing that gets enforced is the stuff that doesn't make anyone mad, which is exactly the problem we identified earlier. I think the real tragedy is that by the time we figure out how to organize ourselves to fight that system, the kids will have already graduated with that "soft" skill set and we'll be stuck trying to hire them for jobs that require grit and critical thinking, not just the ability to scroll. It's a losing battle, so most of us just end up accepting that our kids will have to figure it out on their own in college, if they even get accepted.

That actually does sound pretty discouraging, but I guess that explains why I've never seen any real change in my district either. It just makes me feel like we're stuck in this cycle of accepting mediocrity because nobody wants to do the hard work of organizing to fight it. It's just so frustrating to think about my own kids growing up knowing nothing about grit or real research when the whole system is set up to let them slide by. I feel like maybe we've already lost that window of opportunity forever, and we'll just be stuck with a generation that can't handle the real world once they leave school. What about you? Do you feel like we're just going to watch them struggle in college, or do you think there's still a tiny chance we can turn this around before it's too late?

I know it's easy to feel like we've completely lost the battle, but I'd actually argue there's still a tiny chance to turn this around if we stop waiting for a top-down fix and start creating our own pressure points at the grassroots level. I've started talking to a few parents in my building who are organizing "shadow learning" groups to supplement the curriculum, so maybe if we build the grit and the research skills outside of school, we can force the system to catch up eventually. It's a long shot, but is it worse than just sitting here watching them slide?

Oh wow, that "shadow learning" idea actually sounds kind of terrifying to hear, but I guess if it means my kids are actually doing the heavy lifting on their own, then maybe that's better than just watching them drift? It just feels so risky to be the parent who pushes them to do extra work while everyone else is letting them off the hook, like I'm going to get the blame if they burn out or get mad at me. But honestly, you make a good point that if we just sit here and do nothing, we're definitely going to be stuck with a generation that can't handle the real world. Do you think those groups are actually getting big enough to make a difference, or are they just a tiny handful of parents trying to keep their own kids afloat?

You make a good point that sitting idle is definitely a losing game, but I have to be honest, I'm a little worried about you taking on the whole burden of "shadow learning" alone. My kids' teachers already feel stretched thin managing the basic classroom chaos, and I'm terrified that if I push them to do independent research or heavy reading, they'll just end up isolated and overwhelmed while their friends at the other end of the spectrum get all the A's without lifting a finger. It feels like an unfair lottery for the students where success depends entirely on whether their parents are willing to fight the battles at school for them, whereas I'd rather see a system-wide shift that makes everyone responsible so no single family has to carry the weight of the entire curriculum gap. Do you really think you have the time and energy to build that whole supplemental curriculum from scratch while trying to keep up with your job, or do you have a team of parents actually helping you design these programs?

You make a really good point about me trying to carry the whole weight alone, honestly. I definitely don't have a whole team of parents designing a curriculum with me, and I'm scared that if I just start forcing my kid to read those heavy textbooks while everyone else is letting them scroll, she's just going to feel completely isolated and freak out. It feels so unfair that her success would depend entirely on me being the only one willing to push her, whereas the other kids just get an easy ride. I guess I'm just worried that by trying to make up for the system's failure, I'm just going to burn myself out and my kid is going to resent me for it. Do you think we should just wait and see what happens, or are you really serious about starting these groups right now?

I get that the isolation factor is terrifying, and honestly, I'm not sure we have the luxury of waiting around to see if a few of us can build a whole curriculum from scratch while holding down full-time jobs; if my kids have to become their own schools just to get a basic education, that feels like a broken system to me. But I'm not ready to just hand over the reins to the status quo either, because if we don't start somewhere, we're definitely going to be stuck in that "soft skill" trap forever. Do you think it's realistic to start small, maybe just one group in my neighborhood, rather than trying to convince the whole district to change overnight? I feel like if we can just prove to a few parents that this supplemental work actually results in better grades and more focus, maybe we can create the momentum to pressure the schools to follow suit without having to carry every single kid on our own shoulders.

I hear you, and honestly, starting small with just a neighborhood group does sound way less scary than trying to save the whole district at once. If we can just get a few families in my area together who are willing to actually read the textbooks and do the projects, maybe we can prove to the school that it's not too late for my kids, and that other parents see they're actually succeeding. It would be nice to know I'm not the only one fighting this battle if my daughter's grades start going up because of it, rather than feeling like I'm just pushing her into a corner while everyone else lets her slide. Do you think finding just two or three other moms in your building who are as stressed out as I am would be enough to start something like that?
